subject: Archaeology
title: Side-Scan Sonar: Mapping the Invisible
description: Learn Side-Scan Sonar: Mapping the Invisible in one minute.

hook.text: Sonar can reveal a shipwreck hidden under sand and mud without anyone getting wet. Sound sees what eyes cannot.

buildup.text: Side-scan sonar tows a sensor behind a ship, sending sound waves sideways across the seabed and recording the echoes.

discovery.text: The resulting images show objects on the bottom in remarkable detail — cannons, anchors.

twist.text: Most 'wrecks' detected by sonar turn out to be rocks or modern debris. False positives waste months of dive time.

climax.text: Multibeam sonar now creates 3D seabed maps accurate to inches. Entire coastlines can be surveyed in days.

punchline.text: We can now map the ocean floor like a city street. Most of it is still unmapped.

quiz.question: What is a major challenge with side-scan sonar wreck detection?
options: Sound waves cannot penetrate deeper than 100 feet
Most detected objects turn out to be rocks or debris, not wrecks
Sonar only works in warm tropical waters

details.summary: Side-scan sonar creates detailed acoustic images of the seafloor by emitting sound pulses and measuring reflections. It can detect shipwrecks, submerged structures, and geological features across vast areas, often revealing sites invisible to divers and too deep for direct observation.
details.whyItMatters: Side-scan sonar made systematic underwater survey possible. Before it, finding wrecks was largely accidental. Now entire regions can be mapped acoustically, revealing hundreds of sites that would otherwise remain hidden forever.
takeaways: Side-scan sonar creates acoustic images of the seafloor
It can detect wrecks and structures across vast survey areas
The technology made systematic underwater survey possible

faq.question: How does side-scan sonar work?
faq.answer: A torpedo-shaped instrument (towfish) is towed behind a vessel, emitting fan-shaped sound pulses to each side. Reflections from the seafloor create detailed images showing objects, textures, and shadows. Shipwrecks, anchors, and even individual artifacts can be identified from the acoustic returns.

faq.question: Can sonar replace diving for underwater archaeology?
faq.answer: Not entirely. Sonar is excellent for finding and mapping sites but cannot replace hands-on excavation for recording and recovering artifacts. It works best as a survey tool that identifies promising targets for subsequent diver or ROV investigation.
